name: Belle Isle Park
label: Belle Isle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'James Scott Memorial Fountain' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'James Scott Memorial Fountain' (relation/9146545): middle (105 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14903749: large area 'Belle Isle' (4756 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Island park with conservatory, fountain and skyline views.

text.description: Belle Isle Park is a 982-acre island park in the Detroit River, reached from the city by the MacArthur Bridge. Frederick Law Olmsted, who designed Central Park in New York, was hired in the 1880s to plan it, though only some of his design was finished. The island has a lot to see: an aquarium and conservatory by Albert Kahn, a marble lighthouse at the east end, beaches and plenty of shoreline. For a phone photo, start at the James Scott Memorial Fountain. Cass Gilbert designed it and it was completed in 1925. Seen from the front, the spray and marble figures sit in the foreground with the Detroit skyline rising behind them, so one frame holds the island and the city. It is a popular place for wedding and portrait photos, and sunset is the favoured hour. Two other spots are worth a look if you have time. Sunset Point shows the skyline and river at dusk, with the Ambassador Bridge and Windsor's shoreline across the water. Belle Isle Front Beach has open river and trees, with Windsor in the distance. Work on the fountain is under way. One guide says the plaza and nearby areas are closed through 2026, but the fountain can still be photographed from outside the closed area. Please check the current position before you travel.
text.geographic_location: Belle Isle is an island in the Detroit River, just off mainland Detroit and joined to it by the MacArthur Bridge. The border with Canada runs along the channel to the south of the island.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are given for this spot, so start from downtown Detroit and go to the MacArthur Bridge, which is the road link to the island. Check local transport options for reaching the MacArthur Bridge. Once on the island, head for the James Scott Memorial Fountain and follow the park signs. If you are driving, check the state park's vehicle entry requirements before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the skyline behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole fountain and more sky, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the skyline closer behind the spray.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (view from the front, with the downtown skyline behind the fountain). The fountain's spray and marble figures in the foreground, with the Detroit skyline rising behind it. If the plaza is still closed, shoot from the nearest open spot outside the closed area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain on one side, with the skyline along the upper line. Keep the horizon level. For a wider, cleaner frame, try 0.5x from low down. If you have time, Sunset Point is a good second spot for the skyline and river at dusk.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours are not washed out. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the spray. Use portrait mode if you are photographing people in front of the fountain, and night mode once the light fades, holding the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the sun is low and the skyline glows.

text.access_note: Belle Isle is a Michigan state park and a Recreation Passport is needed for vehicles. The fountain area is under renovation, so check the official site before you go.

name: Eastern Market
label: Eastern Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dequindre Cut Greenway' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dequindre Cut Greenway' (way/8756047): point nearest the subject (2480 m long).
pin_note: Position from OSM W581362401 (Eastern Market): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic public market with murals.

text.description:
Eastern Market is a working market district, and the best phone photo here is not taken inside the sheds. It is taken from the northern end of the Dequindre Cut Greenway, next to the market. The greenway runs sunken below street level, and its walls are covered in murals. People cycle and skate past them, and the market's industrial surroundings sit behind. That mix of colourful street art, movement and industrial background makes a lively, very local picture.

The usual advice is to shoot down onto riders passing a mural. Looking down gives you the painted wall, the path and the people in one frame. If you want the market itself, the shed walls also carry colourful murals, and they make a good backdrop for vendors and shoppers with the open sheds visible. Lincoln Street Art Park is a quieter street-art setting near the market, if the sheds feel crowded.

Saturday is the busiest day, so go early if you want space. Vendors are usually happy to be photographed if you buy something and ask first. Photographing people in public is generally legal, but using a recognisable person's image commercially needs their release.
text.geographic_location: Eastern Market is a market district in Detroit. The Dequindre Cut Greenway meets it at its northern end.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so head to the northern end of the Dequindre Cut Greenway, next to Eastern Market. From there the market sheds are about 240 m to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for riders and the mural together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole painted wall and the cut below. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single rider from where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Dequindre Cut Greenway (northern end near Eastern Market; bridges above the cut). Murals on the sunken greenway walls with cyclists and skaters passing, framed against the market's industrial surroundings. If there is a bridge nearby, shoot down from it onto the mural wall and the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the mural along one third of the frame, leaving the path for riders to cross. If you shoot from a bridge, lean slightly over the rail, without dropping your phone, to keep the wall straight. For a second picture, walk to the market sheds and frame a mural behind the stalls, or try Lincoln Street Art Park for a quieter wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rider's path to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the mural colours stay rich and the bright sky does not wash out. Try a Live Photo so you can pick the best frame as a cyclist passes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when light falls into the cut at an angle. For the market sheds, go early on a Saturday, but expect crowds.

text.access_note: The Dequindre Cut Greenway is an open public path, but check the official site before you go for current market arrangements.

name: Ford Field
label: Ford Field
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brush Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Brush Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/110555613: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ford Field' (390 m across).
notes: Home of the Detroit Lions.

text.description: Ford Field is the indoor stadium of the Detroit Lions, set on the edge of Downtown Detroit next to Comerica Park. It is a big building, and the outline on the map is about 390 m across, so the photo is about how you fit it into the frame. From there the stadium sits on one side of the street, and the long roadway leads your eye along its front. The stadium was built around an old Hudson's warehouse from the 1920s, which is now offices. The playing field is sunk 45 feet (14 m) below street level, which helps keep the stadium from towering over the skyline. The frosted windows near the roofline are meant to echo Detroit's car factories. Super Bowl XL was played here on 5 February 2006. Stand on the pavement, keep the road leading into the picture, and let the stadium fill one side. Brush Street is busy on game days, so a quieter day is easier for photos. If you have time, the corner of Brush Street and Adams Street shows the curved glass entrance.
text.geographic_location: Ford Field is in Downtown Detroit, next to Comerica Park, on the north-east side of the stand-here point on Brush Street.
text.directions_text: Head for Downtown Detroit and walk to Brush Street, on the stretch across from Comerica Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the stadium front will not fit, and use 2x if you want to pick out a detail such as the marquee.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Brush Street (the stretch across from Comerica Park, looking toward the stadium). Ford Field on one side of the street, framed down the Brush Street roadway, with Comerica Park across from it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the line of the road to lead the eye towards the stadium. Keep your phone level so the building edges stay straight. For a close-up of the curved glass entrance with the Ford Field marquee, try the corner of Brush Street and Adams Street instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stadium wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Hold the phone still, or lean against a post for steadiness.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a day with no Lions game or event, in daylight, when the street is quieter and easier to shoot. Check the stadium's event calendar before you go.

text.access_note: Brush Street is a public street, but it is closed on Lions game days for the pregame gathering, and entry to the stadium itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Days without games or events are likely to be quieter on Brush Street than game days.
Daylight is easier for street-level photos of the stadium front than darkness.

name: Detroit Institute of Arts
label: Detroit Institute of A
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1553447: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Detroit Institute of Arts' (256 m across).
notes: Art museum famous for Diego Rivera's Detroit Industry murals.

text.description:
The Detroit Institute of Arts, usually called the DIA, is one of the largest art museums in the United States. It has over 100 galleries and a collection of more than 65,000 works, from ancient Egyptian pieces to contemporary art. The original building was designed by Paul Philippe Cret, with north and south wings on either side. White marble covers the whole exterior, which gives a clean, pale subject against the sky. A major renovation and expansion finished in 2007. The museum's first painting was donated in 1883, and it sits in Detroit's Cultural Center Historic District.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the broad marble frontage and its calm, symmetrical look. The building is very wide, so the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) is the easiest way to fit the wings and the central block into one frame. Use the gridlines to keep the rooflines level, because tilting the phone makes a formal building look as if it is leaning. Once you are happy with the wide view, switch to the default lens (1x) or a little zoom for a tighter shot of the marble detail.

Inside, Diego Rivera's Detroit Industry frescoes surround the central grand court. Photography rules inside can differ from the outside, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Midtown Detroit, in the Cultural Center Historic District, about 3.2 km north of downtown. It stands across from the Detroit Public Library and close to Wayne State University.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so start from downtown Detroit and head north for about 3.2 km, towards Midtown. The Detroit Public Library is across from the museum, so look for it as a landmark. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the wide marble building into the frame. Then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, or 2x to pick out architectural detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof edge with a horizontal line so the building stays straight. Keep the phone level and at chest height. If the whole width does not fit, step back a few paces rather than tilting the phone upwards. Take one wide shot, then a closer one of the marble and the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white marble keeps its detail and does not turn into a flat white patch.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits white marble best, as it avoids the harsh glare of midday.

text.access_note: The grounds and building front can be seen from outside, but entry to the museum and any photography rules inside may vary, so check the official site before you go.

photo.from: Own photo, taken 7 m from the phone icon

name: Motown Museum
label: Motown Museum
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 23 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 55 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/105533840: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Motown Museum' (40 m across).
notes: Original Motown Records studio.

text.description:
This small house on West Grand Boulevard was Motown's first headquarters and recording studio, nicknamed Hitsville U.S.A. Berry Gordy bought it in 1959 and turned the back of the old photographers' studio into a recording room. The Gordy family lived upstairs at first. Within a few years the label had taken over several neighbouring houses. Today the Motown Museum occupies the original house and an adjacent former residence, and has done so since 1985. Inside, Studio A has been kept as it was, and an 1877 Steinway grand piano is on display there.

It photographs well because of the contrast: a very ordinary-looking house with an extraordinary story. That makes it a good subject for a simple, honest street photo rather than a grand view. Take one wide shot to show the house in its street, then a closer one of the front for detail.

The museum is a popular stop, so people may walk through your frame. Wait a moment for a gap, or include a few figures to show the scale of the house.
text.geographic_location: The Motown Museum is at 2648 West Grand Boulevard, near the New Center area of Detroit. The stretch of road where it stands has been renamed Berry Gordy Jr. Boulevard.
text.directions_text: From the New Center area, take a taxi or hired scooter to 2648 West Grand Boulevard, as no station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The museum is 50 m to the east of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole house. Try 2x for a tighter shot of the front, and use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer and cannot fit the frontage in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (On the sidewalk in front of the brick facade on West Grand Boulevard (also signed Berry Gordy Jr. Boulevard here), framing the house and the Motown sign). The brick Hitsville U.S.A. house facade with the Motown sign out front, the classic exterior shot of the museum.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the house's vertical edges lined up with them so the walls don't lean. Hold the phone level at chest height rather than tilting it up. Leave a little street in the foreground to show the setting, then take a second, closer frame of the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the house to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls stay detailed instead of washing out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on a bright overcast day suits it well. On a sunny day, afternoon light should be behind you when you look east, though check that nothing is casting shade on the front.

text.access_note: The museum is a visitor attraction and entry is likely to be ticketed, so check the official site before you go, including any rules on photography inside; the outside can be photographed from the street.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is on or beside the street, so the view east is a normal street-level view of the building's frontage.
The house is modest and ordinary-looking from the outside.
Visitors and passers-by may walk through the frame at busy times.
In the afternoon the sun is in the west, so it would be behind someone looking east, though shade from nearby buildings or trees is possible.
Entry to the museum is probably ticketed and interior photography may be restricted.

name: Comerica Park
label: Comerica Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Grand Circus Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Grand Circus Park' (relation/10012029): middle (280 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1307250153: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Comerica Park' (440 m across).
notes: Home of the Detroit Tigers.

text.description: Comerica Park is the open-air home of the Detroit Tigers baseball team, opened in 2000 and built in a retro-classic style. It seats 41,083 people and sits right in the middle of downtown, so it photographs well as part of the city rather than as a building on its own. From Grand Circus Park, the green space and paved walks lead your eye towards the ballpark, with downtown buildings framing the stadium. Approach from the Woodward Avenue side, where the ballpark comes into view across a parking lot. The park also has statues and historic architecture that make good extra subjects while you are there. The classic close-up is at the main entrance, where a tiger statue 15 feet (4.6 m) tall stands guard. The entrance faces the Fox Theatre and sits between two historic churches, St. John Episcopal Church and Central United Methodist Church, so a wider shot can include some of that old brickwork. Eight other large tiger statues are inside the park, and 33 tiger heads with lit-up baseballs in their mouths line the brick walls outside. The stadium is expected to be renamed Fifth Third Park before the 2027 season, so signs may change. Do both views if you have time: first the wide frame from the park, then walk over for the tiger. Game days bring crowds and possible closures, so allow extra time and be patient for a clear shot.
text.geographic_location: Comerica Park is in downtown Detroit, close to Grand Circus Park and the Fox Theatre. Its main entrance lies between two historic downtown churches.
text.directions_text: Start from downtown Detroit and head for Grand Circus Park. Walk towards the Woodward Avenue side and the ballpark will come into view across a parking lot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view of the park with the ballpark beyond. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the tiger statue up close, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the stadium from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Grand Circus Park (approach from the Woodward Avenue side, where the ballpark comes into view across a parking lot). A wide view of the park's green space and paved walks with the ballpark visible beyond, framing the stadium with downtown architecture. The ballpark is to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the path or lawn in the lower third, with the stadium on one of the upper lines. Keep the buildings straight by holding the phone level. As an alternative, go to the main entrance and crouch low with the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens, so the tiger statue fills the foreground and the stadium gate sits behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stadium to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the brickwork and statue keep their colour. Use portrait mode on the tiger only if you are standing a few steps back.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the stadium from the park. Early evening can add warmer light and a livelier feel. Avoid game-day crowds if you want an empty frame.

text.access_note: Grand Circus Park is a public park, but the ballpark itself is ticketed for games and may have closures on event days, so check the official site before you go.

name: Fisher Building
label: Fisher Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cadillac Place' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cadillac Place' (way/778011537): middle (259 m across); moved 35 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/112057847: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fisher Building' (190 m across).
notes: Art Deco landmark with a copper-green roof.

text.description: The Fisher Building is a 30-storey Art Deco office tower in Detroit's New Center area, finished in 1928 and designed by Albert Kahn's firm. It is faced with limestone, granite and several kinds of marble, and it has been called "Detroit's largest art object". The roof is the part that catches the eye: the hipped roof was first covered in gold leaf tiles, which were later replaced with green ones, and coloured lights have made them look golden at night since the 1980s. The tower stands 428 feet (130 m) to the roof, so it rewards a vertical frame. From the entrance portico you can look across the street and see the tower and its upper facade rising above the road, with the neighbouring Kahn-designed building framing one side. Photographers often pair the two Kahn buildings from here. Hold the phone upright, use the gridlines to keep the tower straight, and leave some sky above the roof. Stepping back along the pavement gives you a little more room. Exterior views from public sidewalks are fine, but the portico depends on current access, so check before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Fisher Building is at 3011 West Grand Boulevard in the New Center area of Detroit, north of downtown. It stands directly across the boulevard from Cadillac Place, the former General Motors Building.
text.directions_text: No nearby stations or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the New Center area of Detroit. Cadillac Place is on West Grand Boulevard. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the tower with the street and the neighbouring building. Switch to the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the roof and upper stages. The ultra-wide (0.5x) can fit the whole tower from close by, but the sides will lean inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Cadillac Place (entrance portico, across West Grand Boulevard from the Fisher). The Fisher's tower and upper facade rising over the street, framed by the neighboring Kahn-designed building. Face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright, switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line. Include a strip of the neighbouring building on one side as a frame, and keep the roof clear of the top edge. For a different view, try Second Avenue and Lothrop Street for the corner and eastern end of the north face from street level. Second Avenue and Bethune Street shows the roofline and tower from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower's stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a post or your body to catch the lit roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk and the evening, when the roof tiles are lit. In daylight, the facade is easier to read when you are not shooting straight into the sun.

text.access_note: Exterior views are from public sidewalks, but whether the Cadillac Place portico is open depends on the building's current access, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Dusk and evening are good times because the roof lights are on and the sky is darker.
Daylight shooting is easier when not facing directly into the sun.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) makes the sides of a tall building lean inwards.
Stepping back along the pavement gives a little more room for the shot.

name: Campus Martius Park
label: Campus Martius Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Campus Martius Park' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/107622369: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Campus Martius Park' (135 m across).
notes: Central downtown square with an ice rink in winter.

text.description:
Campus Martius Park is a small, lively public square in the middle of downtown Detroit, and it is an easy place to take good phone photos. The central lawn and the Woodward Fountain sit in front of a ring of downtown towers, so you get open space in the foreground and tall buildings behind. The setting changes with the seasons. In summer there is beach-style seating on the lawn, and in winter the park has the holiday tree and the ice rink. Both are popular backdrops.

The park was dedicated on 19 November 2004 and covers 1.2 acres. It is a re-creation of an older square that was lost when downtown was reshaped for traffic. It is also the point of origin of Detroit's coordinate system, marked by a medallion set into the stone walkway at the western point of the diamond around the Woodward Fountain. That makes a nice close-up detail shot if you find it. The Michigan Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument, a Civil War-era memorial, is nearby and gives you another subject.

For your photos, stand on the lawn near the Woodward Fountain and look across the park. Put the fountain in the lower part of the frame and let the towers fill the background. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. If you want a higher view, the Millender Center parking structure looks over Cadillac Square towards the park, but check that the roof is open to visitors before you go up.
text.geographic_location: Campus Martius Park is in Downtown Detroit, at the meeting of Woodward Avenue and Michigan Avenue. It is four blocks south of Grand Circus Park, and Cadillac Square Park lies directly to its east.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The park sits at the intersection of Woodward Avenue and Michigan Avenue in Downtown Detroit. Grand Circus Park is four blocks to the north, which is a useful landmark if you are walking down Woodward Avenue. The phone icon on the map is inside the park itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lawn, fountain and towers together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the skyline, or if the park is busy and you need to stand close. Use 2x or more for details such as the fountain spray or the medallion in the walkway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the central lawn and fountain with the downtown towers behind them. In winter you also see the holiday tree and the ice rink.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on a lower line, with the towers filling the top third. Keep the phone upright and level so the buildings stay straight. The Millender Center parking structure gives a higher view over Cadillac Square towards the park, if the roof is open to visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the buildings keep their detail. Try a Live Photo of the fountain water and pick the best frame afterwards. In winter evenings, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body for the tree lights.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose the season you prefer: summer for the beach-style seating, winter for the tree and rink. Seasonal setups change, so check what is currently on.

text.access_note: The park is a public open space, but events and seasonal attractions such as the rink may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Detroit Riverwalk
label: Detroit Riverwalk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hart Plaza' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hart Plaza' (way/69349404): middle (409 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1815363: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Waterfront promenade with views across to Windsor.

text.description: The Detroit Riverwalk is the public path along the Detroit River in the middle of the city, and it is part of the wider Detroit International Riverfront, which stretches 5.5 miles from the Ambassador Bridge to Belle Isle. USA Today readers voted it the best riverwalk in the United States in 2021, 2022 and 2023. For a phone photo, the appeal is simple: a long path beside open water, with the city rising behind it. The best-known building here is the Renaissance Center, a group of seven linked towers that has been the tallest building in Michigan since 1977. Looking out from the riverfront, you also get the Windsor shoreline across the water. A good first photo is taken from the riverfront edge of Hart Plaza, where the Riverwalk begins and runs away along the water, with the skyline and the far shore behind it. People leaning on the railing at sunset add scale and life to the frame. If you want something different, walk along the path towards the Renaissance Center and shoot up at the towers with the river and path in the foreground. The riverfront also hosts large events and festivals, so it can be busier than usual on those days. Weekend street parking nearby is reported to be tight, so arriving on foot or by taxi is easier.
text.geographic_location: The Riverwalk runs along the Detroit River in downtown Detroit. The Hart Plaza section sits right beside the Renaissance Center, where the path begins.
text.directions_text: Head for the Renaissance Center on the downtown riverfront and ask for Hart Plaza, which is next to it. Go to the river side of the plaza, where the Riverwalk starts. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the river, the skyline and the far shore. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move closer to the Renaissance Center and want the towers in the frame. The telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out people at the railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hart Plaza (the riverfront edge of the plaza, where the Riverwalk begins). The Riverwalk running along the water with the skyline and the Windsor shoreline behind, with people at the railing at sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the Riverwalk railing along a lower line so the path leads the eye along the river. Keep the horizon level and leave room for the skyline and sky. For an alternative, walk along the Riverwalk towards the Renaissance Center and use the ultra-wide to fill the frame with the towers, with the path and river in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour at sunset. If people are walking by, a Live Photo or a burst makes it easier to catch a good moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when people line the rail with the river and skyline behind them.

text.access_note: This is a public riverside walkway and plaza, but events and festivals are held on the riverfront, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Windsor, Canada, is on the opposite side of the Detroit River from downtown Detroit.
Hart Plaza and the Renaissance Center are in downtown Detroit.
The riverfront may be busier than usual during large events and festivals.

name: Guardian Building
label: Guardian Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Griswold Street and Congress Street corner' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Griswold Street and Congress Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/330839648: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Guardian Building' (105 m across).
notes: Art Deco skyscraper known for its colourful lobby.

text.description: The Guardian Building is a 43-story office tower in downtown Detroit's Financial District. It was built in 1928-29 as the Union Trust Building and is a bold piece of Art Deco design. Its nickname, the Cathedral of Finance, comes from its cathedral-like tower over the main entrance. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1989 and is now owned by Wayne County. It photographs well because the outside is so colourful: warm orange brick, tile, limestone and terra cotta are set in geometric patterns instead of plain decoration. The main frame rises 32 stories, topped by two uneven spires, the taller reaching about 193 m (632 ft). The base is granite and stone, and two sculptures by Corrado Parducci flank the Griswold Street entrance. From the corner of Griswold Street and Congress Street you can see the orange north face with its huge arched window and coloured tile surround, and the whole tower climbing above it. Start wide to take in the full height, then move in for the brickwork and tile. If you want a different view, Campus Martius Park gives a wider shot of the tower over the downtown streets, and the corner of Griswold Street and Larned Street shows the tiled entrance area at an angle. The best-known pictures are of the lobby, which is a separate matter from this exterior view.
text.geographic_location: The Guardian Building stands on Griswold Street in the Financial District of downtown Detroit.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Financial District in downtown Detroit and make for the corner of Griswold Street and Congress Street, with the building to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the tower and the big arched window into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the north face. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tile surround and the stone courses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Griswold Street and Congress Street (diagonally across the intersection from the building's corner). The orange brick north face with the three-story arched window and its colored tile surround, with the full height of the tower rising above the corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone upright so the tower's edges stay straight. Put the arched window in the lower-middle of the frame and let the tower rise above it. Wait for a gap in the traffic and pedestrians. For a different view, try Campus Martius Park for a wider full-height shot, or move to the Griswold Street and Larned Street corner for the tiled entrance area.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the orange stays rich. If the tower looks tilted in the ultra-wide, step back and shoot at 1x instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Bright daylight shows the brick and tile colours best. Avoid very harsh midday sun, which can make the stonework look flat.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public pavement; the building is an office with a lobby, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Michigan Central Station
label: Michigan Central
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Roosevelt Park' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Roosevelt Park' (relation/11809325): middle (375 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7745389962: the OpenStreetMap point 'Michigan Central Station'.
notes: Restored Beaux-Arts railway station in Corktown.

text.description:
Michigan Central Station is a Beaux-Arts railway building in Corktown, finished in 1913-14 as Detroit's main intercity station. It has a train hall and a 230-foot (70 m) office tower. When it was built it was the tallest railway station in the world. The last trains left in January 1988, and for years the empty building was one of the best-known ruins in the United States. Ford bought it in 2018, and after a restoration costing more than $900 million it reopened on 6 June 2024.

It photographs well because the whole front is clear of clutter. From Roosevelt Park, on the north side, you look straight at the main facade and entrance, with lawns and paths leading the eye towards the building. The tall stone tower rising behind the lower hall gives a strong, simple shape that reads well even on a small phone screen.

Stand on the park paths and give yourself some space. The building is a fair distance away, so the whole front fits in the frame without any tricks. For a different view, try Michigan Avenue, where the station stands at the end of the street, or 15th Street, which shows the northeast side filling the frame. Building work or event set-ups can change what you see, so look at the current conditions when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: In the Corktown district of Detroit, about 1.2 km south-west of downtown and near the Ambassador Bridge. The station sits behind Roosevelt Park, which forms its front lawn.
text.directions_text: From downtown Detroit, head south-west to Corktown and Roosevelt Park, on the north side of the station. Please check the current layout of the area and your route before you go, as work or events nearby may change the way in. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole facade, tower and lawns. Switch to 2x or the telephoto lens to pick out the tower and the carved stonework. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk closer and want the full height of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Roosevelt Park (front (north) side of the station, across the park paths). The station's main facade and entrance framed by the restored park lawns and paths.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the entrance on the centre line, with a park path leading towards it if you can. Keep the phone level so the tower stays upright. Leave a band of lawn in the foreground for depth. For a second view, try Michigan Avenue, which shows the station standing alone at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames at 1x and 2x so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light falls on the windows and the weathered stone. Summer weekends can be busy, so go earlier if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: Roosevelt Park is a free public park, but check the official site before you go for station access, event closures and any rules for photography inside.

name: Renaissance Center
label: Renaissance Center
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10011997: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Renaissance Center' (442 m across).
notes: Seven-tower glass complex on the riverfront.

text.description:
The Renaissance Center, known locally as the RenCen, is the cluster of glass towers that dominates Detroit's riverfront. It has seven connected towers. The tallest is a round 74-storey hotel in the middle, the tallest building in Michigan, and four office towers stand around it. Developed in the 1970s as a 'city-within-a-city', it was designed by architect John Portman. The first five towers opened in 1976-77, and two shorter ones followed in 1981. A glass atrium called the Wintergarden was added in the early 2000s, opening the complex up to the riverfront.

It photographs well because the shapes are so simple. A tall cylinder is ringed by smaller towers, and the glass picks up the sky. Tilt the phone upwards slowly and watch the vertical lines. Gridlines help keep the towers straight.

The complex has been changing. General Motors moved its headquarters out in early 2026, and part of the site is planned for demolition and redevelopment, so the view and access may differ from older photos. Check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Renaissance Center stands on the Detroit International Riverfront in downtown Detroit, beside the river.
text.directions_text: Head for the Renaissance Center on the downtown riverfront; if you are not already in downtown Detroit, go by taxi or hired scooter. Walk to the southern side and stop where the towers rise directly ahead of you to the north. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tall central tower and its neighbours into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line one of the vertical edges of the towers up with a grid line. Hold the phone level, not tilted back, to keep the sides straight. Leave some sky above the round tower so it does not look cut off, and try a lower angle with a little foreground in the frame to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the towers keep their detail. With the ultra-wide (0.5x), keep people and objects away from the edges of the frame, where they look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late morning to mid-afternoon can light the glass facing you. Around sunset the glass picks up warm colour, and just after dusk night mode can capture the lit towers against a deep blue sky. Hold the phone steady against something solid for night shots.

text.access_note: The surrounding riverfront is an outdoor public area, but access to the buildings and plaza may change as the site is redeveloped, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is on the southern side of the complex, so you look north towards the towers.
The walk from the middle of the complex to the stand-here point takes about 2 minutes (107 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
From the south side, the sun is mostly behind or beside you around midday, which usually lights the glass facing you.
The glass picks up warm colour around sunset, and the towers are lit after dark.
The riverfront area around the complex is generally an outdoor public space, though access may change during redevelopment.

name: Fox Theatre
label: Fox Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Woodward Avenue' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Woodward Avenue and West Montcalm Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6150469184: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fox Theatre'.
notes: Lavishly decorated 1928 movie palace.

text.description: The Fox Theatre opened in 1928 as a flagship movie palace and is still one of Detroit's grandest buildings. Architect C. Howard Crane designed it, and with 5,048 seats it is the largest surviving movie palace of the 1920s. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1989 and was fully restored in 1988. From Woodward Avenue you see the ten-storey office building that forms the theatre's front. It is faced in cream terracotta and decorated with Asian-inspired motifs. The theatre's marquee is visible at the base of the façade, so one frame can hold the neon sign, the tall façade and the life of the street. That mix of detail and scale is why it photographs so well. Stand on the Woodward Avenue corner, and look south at the theatre's front. A historic postcard in the Detroit Historical Society archive shows an elevated view of the building from this corner, so a street-level shot only approximates that classic angle, and the original vantage may no longer be open, so check on site. Cars and pedestrians passing in the foreground add scale and a sense of the city. If you want a closer shot, walk the short distance to the main entrance and photograph the marquee at eye level. Keep to the outside of the building: photography is not permitted in the side of the theatre or backstage.
text.geographic_location: The Fox Theatre is at 2211 Woodward Avenue in Downtown Detroit, close to the Grand Circus Park Historic District. The surrounding area is nicknamed Foxtown.
text.directions_text: Head for the Grand Circus Park area of Downtown Detroit, then follow Woodward Avenue; the Fox is right on it. Ask for 2211 Woodward Avenue or look it up on a map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the ten-storey façade and the marquee from the corner. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the marquee lettering and the terracotta decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Woodward Avenue and West Montcalm Street (the corner where the two streets meet, looking at the theatre's front). The Fox's Woodward-side façade and marquee from the street corner, with traffic and pedestrians in the foreground. The theatre is a very short distance to the south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the edges of the tower up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean. Keep a little street in the bottom of the frame for atmosphere. For a close, eye-level shot of the entrance and neon marquee, walk to the main Woodward entrance as a second viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the marquee to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the neon doesn't wash out to white. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a lamp post or your body. Wait for a gap in the traffic if you want a clean foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the façade and marquee are lit, gives the most dramatic result. In daylight the cream terracotta and its detail show up best.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public street, but inside the theatre access and photography depend on events, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The marquee is lit with neon or bright lights in the evening.
The corner viewpoint is at street level and has passing traffic and pedestrians.
Gridlines help keep tall buildings looking straight in a phone photo.
Montcalm Street is the street that meets Woodward Avenue at the corner just north of the theatre.

name: Detroit Opera House
label: Detroit Opera House
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/55690248: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Detroit Opera House' (106 m across).
notes: Ornate 1922 theatre on Broadway Street.

text.description:
The Detroit Opera House is an ornate theatre on Broadway Street in Downtown Detroit, part of the Grand Circus Park Historic District. It opened on 22 January 1922 as the Capitol Theatre, designed by C. Howard Crane, who also worked on other well-known Detroit theatres. Over the decades it was a cinema with live acts, then the Grand Circus Theatre. It closed in 1978, reopened briefly in 1981, and closed again after a fire in 1985. The Michigan Opera Theatre bought it in 1988. After a long restoration it reopened in 1996 as the Detroit Opera House, and it now seats 2,700. It also appears in the 2012 documentary Detropia.

It photographs well because it is a big, solid, decorated building in a part of the city with several historic theatres close together. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south of the numbered pin. That makes it hard to fit in at the default lens (1x), so the ultra-wide (0.5x) is your friend. Keep your phone upright and level so the vertical lines stay straight, then switch to the default lens (1x) or a little zoom for the details. Look for sign lettering, doorways and decorative stonework. Watch for people and traffic crossing your frame, and take a few shots a few seconds apart.
text.geographic_location: The Detroit Opera House is at 1526 Broadway Street in Downtown Detroit, within the Grand Circus Park Historic District. It sits close to Grand Circus Park, among the city's older theatre buildings.
text.directions_text: No Underground-style station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Downtown Detroit and head for Broadway Street in the Grand Circus Park Historic District. Walk towards it and the building will be straight ahead of you to the north. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long front of the building in from close up. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Stay on the pavement and out of the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so it does not lean. Hold the phone upright, not tilted up, and step back a little if you can to fit more in. Then take a second shot at 2x or more of the signage and decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the lights and bright sky don't wash out. In low light, let night mode run and hold the phone still against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is easiest for seeing the stonework and details. Dusk or early evening can be good for lit signs and warm light, with night mode helping.

text.access_note: The building's exterior can be photographed from the street, but check the official site before you go if you want to see inside or attend a performance.

name: Hart Plaza
label: Hart Plaza
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Horace E. Dodge Fountain' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Horace E. Dodge and Son Memorial Fountain' (node/1215294644): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/69349404: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hart Plaza' (411 m across).
notes: Riverfront plaza with the Dodge Fountain.

text.description: Hart Plaza is Detroit's big riverside plaza, and it makes a good photo stop because it combines sculpture, open space and a city backdrop in one spot. It opened in 1975 and can hold about 40,000 people for concerts and festivals. It sits roughly where Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac landed in 1701 to found the settlement that became Detroit. The centrepiece is the Horace E. Dodge and Son Memorial Fountain, designed by Isamu Noguchi and Walter Budd in 1978. Its water jets rise in the middle of the plaza, with the downtown skyline behind them. That fountain is the shot to go for. It looks best after dark, when it is lit up. Around it you will find other photo subjects: the stainless steel Pylon at the main entrance, the 63-foot steel arch called Transcending, and a bronze statue of Cadillac's arrival. Across the river you can see Windsor, Ontario. For your phone, start with the fountain in the foreground and the skyline behind it. Then walk to the Jefferson Avenue side for a wider view of the plaza's entrance, with the bronze Fist sculpture in the foreground. If you have time, the Detroit Riverwalk gives a view back towards the plaza, with the river and Windsor skyline in the scene. Festivals can crowd or fence off parts of the plaza, so be flexible about where you stand.
text.geographic_location: Hart Plaza is in downtown Detroit on the Detroit River, at the river end of Woodward Avenue. It is bounded by East Jefferson Avenue to the north and sits a few blocks from the Renaissance Center.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from downtown Detroit and head for the river end of Woodward Avenue, where it meets East Jefferson Avenue. If you are coming from further out, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Hart Plaza. The main entrance is at the foot of Woodward Avenue, and the fountain stands near the middle of the plaza, a short walk in from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the fountain's jets and the skyline in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view with less edge stretching. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single jet or the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in the middle of the plaza, standing at the fountain's edge). The Noguchi fountain's water jets in the foreground with the downtown skyline behind, most striking when the fountain is lit at night. Go to the Horace E. From there the water jets fill the foreground and the downtown skyline rises behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the jets low in the frame, with the skyline along the top third. Hold the phone low and level so the buildings stay straight. For a different view, walk to Jefferson Avenue and shoot the plaza's entrance with the bronze Fist sculpture in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest jets to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit water does not turn white. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep still. A Live Photo can capture the moving water and let you pick the best frame later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the fountain is lit.

text.access_note: Hart Plaza is a public plaza, but summer festivals can fence off or crowd parts of it, so check the official site before you go.

name: Spirit of Detroit
label: Spirit of Detroit
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Spirit Plaza' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Spirit of Detroit Plaza' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1293799469: the OpenStreetMap point 'The Spirit of Detroit'.
notes: Landmark bronze statue by the Coleman Young Municipal Center.

text.description:
The Spirit of Detroit is a huge bronze figure, seated and holding a golden sphere in one hand and a small family group in the other. It was made by Marshall Fredericks and dedicated in 1958. It stands about 26 feet (7.9 m) tall in front of the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center, and it is one of the largest bronze statues in the United States. It has become a symbol of the city and appears on many city logos.

It photographs well because the shapes are bold and the colours are simple. The green bronze and the gilded details stand out against the curved white marble wall behind, which carries the seals of the City of Detroit and Wayne County. The wall gives a clean backdrop, so the statue reads clearly even on a busy day. The plaza in front is a wide, open space, so you can move back and forth to change how much of the figure fills the frame.

From here you see the bronze figure with the marble wall and seals behind it, and you can walk closer if you want the figure to fill the frame. It is also the spot most visitors use for portraits, so you may need to wait a moment for a clear shot. During big city events the statue is sometimes dressed in oversized team jerseys, which can change the look of your photo.
text.geographic_location: The statue stands in downtown Detroit at 2 Woodward Ave, on Spirit Plaza in front of the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop is listed for this spot, so start from downtown Detroit and head for the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center at 2 Woodward Ave. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic front view of the figure. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole statue, the marble wall and some of the plaza in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the golden sphere and the small family figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front of the statue, facing it from the plaza). The bronze figure filling the frame from the front, with the curved white marble wall and city seals behind it. The statue is to the north-east. Walk closer if you want the figure to fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the figure on the centre line so the wall sits evenly behind it. Hold the phone level, because tilting it up makes the statue lean backwards. For a wider picture, step back across the plaza and let the GM Building or the downtown skyline rise behind the statue. Another good alternative is from across the street, where you can fit the Joe Louis "The Fist" sculpture into the same photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze figure to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the white marble does not glare. If someone is posing in front, take a few frames or a short Live Photo and pick the cleanest one afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning and late afternoon are suggested for the best light.

text.access_note: Spirit Plaza and the statue are free and open to the public.

name: Penobscot Building
label: Penobscot Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Campus Martius Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Campus Martius Park' (way/107622369): middle (135 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/69000329: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Greater Penobscot Building (1928)' (83 m across).
notes: Art Deco skyscraper in the financial district.

text.description: The Penobscot Building is a 45-storey Art Deco office tower in the heart of downtown Detroit's Financial District. It was built between 1927 and 1928 and stands 566 feet (173 m) tall. It was the tallest building in Detroit and in Michigan until 1977. The architect, Wirt C. Rowland, clad it in Indiana limestone. It rises almost sheer for thirty storeys, then steps back in a series of setbacks to a tower topped with a red beacon. That stepped outline is what makes it work so well in a phone photo: the shape reads clearly even against a busy skyline. From Campus Martius Park, the tower rises above the fountain and the surrounding downtown buildings, so you can get a lively foreground and a clear landmark in one frame. The building is also lit at night. On holidays the lights change colour, and at Christmas the broadcast tower glows gold. If you want a different view, the corner of Griswold Street and West Fort Street shows the whole facade with neighbouring towers beside it. The building is a private office block, so keep your photography to the outside and the park.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Detroit's Financial District, on the Penobscot Block at Griswold Street and West Fort Street. Campus Martius Park is a short walk to the north-east.
text.directions_text: Head for Campus Martius Park in downtown Detroit. From there the Penobscot Building is to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot. Look for the stepped tower with the red beacon on top. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the fountain, the park and the whole tower in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the stepped top and the beacon.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Campus Martius Park. The tower rising above the park's fountain and surrounding downtown buildings, with the Penobscot as the dominant landmark. For an alternative, try the corner of Griswold Street and West Fort Street, which shows the full facade with neighbouring towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain or a park feature in the lower third, with the tower rising behind it. Hold the phone level, then tilt up only slightly, because tilting a lot makes the sides lean inwards. Wait for people to walk through the foreground if you want a sense of life in the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky just above the tower's top to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the limestone keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out. At dusk, use night mode and brace your phone against something solid or hold your elbows tight to your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk. The tower's upper floors are lit at night, and holidays bring colour changes, so staying until after dark can add something extra.

text.access_note: Campus Martius Park is an open public space, but the Penobscot is a private office building with restricted interior photography, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Campus Martius Park has a fountain and is an open public park.
Interior photography in the Penobscot Building is restricted by security.
Late afternoon to dusk is a good time to photograph the tower.
Tilting the phone sharply upwards makes vertical lines lean inwards.
The Griswold Street and West Fort Street corner shows the full facade with neighbouring towers.

name: Monument to Joe Louis
label: Joe Louis Fist
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Woodward Avenue and Jefferson Avenue' (5 web pages); placed at crossing of Woodward Avenue and Jefferson Avenue (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1216215953: the OpenStreetMap point 'Monument to Joe Louis'.
notes: Giant bronze fist sculpture.

text.description: The Monument to Joe Louis, often called The Fist, is a huge bronze forearm and clenched fist hanging from a pyramid-shaped metal frame, in the middle of one of downtown Detroit's busiest junctions. It honours the boxer Joe Louis and stands for the power of his punch, in the ring and outside it. Because Louis fought against Jim Crow laws, the fist was also meant as a statement against racism. The sculptor was Robert Graham, and the piece was a gift from Sports Illustrated, dedicated on 16 October 1986. The arm is 24 feet (7.3 m) long and the frame is 24 feet high. The arm alone weighs 5,000 pounds, and the whole thing with its frame weighs 8,000 pounds. It points towards Canada, which is said to be deliberate. It photographs well because the shape is bold and simple, and the downtown towers behind it show how big the fist really is. The best classic view is from across the street, where the fist seems to be reaching out to bump the viewer. The Spirit of Detroit statue is across the same street, so you can photograph both in one visit. The sculpture is lit at night. Traffic here is busy, so take your photos from the pavement and cross only at the crossings. For a different view, try Hart Plaza nearby, with the fist in front and the river behind. You can also go close to the bronze knuckles and shoot upwards under the arm.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Detroit, on a median where Jefferson Avenue meets Woodward Avenue, close to Hart Plaza and the riverfront.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot, so head for downtown Detroit and the area around Hart Plaza, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. The monument is at the Jefferson Avenue and Woodward Avenue intersection, near Hart Plaza. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fist and pyramid frame seen head-on. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full frame and more of the towers, or to 2x telephoto to pick out the knuckles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Woodward Avenue and Jefferson Avenue (across the street from the monument, on the corner side opposite the sculpture). The bronze arm and pyramid frame seen head-on from across the intersection, with the fist's scale made clear by the nearby downtown towers. The monument is to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the arm up with the frame so it looks straight. Keep a little space around the fist so the towers behind show its scale. Stay low and shoot slightly upwards to make the fist look as if it is reaching towards you. If you want a close-up of the knuckles and the underside of the arm, a second viewpoint is the monument itself, but only if you can reach it safely. Hart Plaza gives a wider view with the river behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not turn white. Try a Live Photo to catch passing traffic. If you stay for the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a post or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset.

text.access_note: The monument stands on a median at a busy junction and is listed as open 24 hours with no admission fee, but how easy it is to get to the base can vary, so check on the day and take care with traffic.
claims_not_in_sources: Low sun around sunrise or sunset gives the bronze a warmer look and softer shadows.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit both the fist and the towers into one frame from across a wide junction.

text.description: Grand Circus Park is a small, half-moon-shaped green space in the middle of Downtown Detroit, covering about 5 acres. It links the theatre district with the financial district. Woodward Avenue, the city's main thoroughfare, cuts through the middle, so you get two halves with a fountain at the heart of each. The city established the park in 1850 as part of Augustus Woodward's plan to rebuild after the 1805 fire. The original idea was a full circle, but that was never completed. The eastern half is anchored by the Russell Alger Memorial Fountain from 1921, designed by Henry Bacon, who also designed the Lincoln Memorial. The western half has the Edison Fountain. Statues of two former mayors, William Cotter Maybury and Hazen Pingree, stand in the park. It photographs well because the fountains, statues and trees give you foreground interest, while tall buildings rise all around. The David Broderick Tower and David Whitney Building are to the south, and the Detroit Opera House and Comerica Park are to the east. Walk around a little before you settle on a view. Try one shot that includes a fountain and a building, and one that is just the open greenery.
text.geographic_location: In Downtown Detroit, about four blocks north of Campus Martius Park. Woodward Avenue runs through the middle of the park, between the theatre district and the financial district.
text.directions_text: Start from Campus Martius Park and head north along Woodward Avenue for about four blocks; the park opens out on both sides of the road. You can also come by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Grand Circus Park. The park is also served by a QLine and People Mover station. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain and its surroundings. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the fountain, the trees and the tall buildings in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the statues or the tops of the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain on one of the lower thirds, so the trees and buildings fill the rest of the frame. Hold the phone low and level to keep the buildings upright. If you want a different view, walk to the western half and look back east, so the Detroit Opera House is behind the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus. If the sky is bright, drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the details do not wash out. Try a Live Photo while the water is moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the tall buildings cast less harsh shade across the park. Weekday midday tends to be busier with people.

text.access_note: The park is a public green space in the city centre, but check the official site before you go if there are events or works nearby.
claims_not_in_sources: The park is an open public space that visitors can walk through freely.
Morning and late-afternoon light is softer than midday light for photography.
Weekday midday is likely to be busier with people.

label: Alger Fountain

notes: Fountain on Harmonie Park Plaza.

text.description:
The Russell Alger Memorial Fountain stands in Grand Circus Park in Detroit and was dedicated on 27 July 1921. It is a bronze Beaux-Arts monument showing a spirited female figure representing Michigan. One hand is raised in greeting and the other holds a sword and shield, with the state crest on the shield in shallow relief. The sculptor was Daniel Chester French and the architect was Henry Bacon, and the bronze was cast by the Gorham Manufacturing Company. Lion heads on the granite base pour water into the bowl around it, and there is a portrait relief of Alger on the base. Russell Alger (1836-1907) rose from private to general in the Civil War, then became Governor of Michigan, a U.S. Senator and U.S. Secretary of War. A society of Civil War veterans commissioned the fountain in his memory.

It photographs well because the figure is tall and sharply outlined, so it reads clearly against trees or sky, and the moving water adds life to the foreground. Take one wide shot that shows the fountain in its park setting, then move in for details such as the raised hand, the shield and the lion heads. Keep your phone level so the granite base does not look as if it is leaning.
text.geographic_location: The fountain is in Grand Circus Park in Detroit.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so head for Grand Circus Park in Detroit, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole fountain from where you stand. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the park around it. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the statue's figure and the lion heads.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The whole monument fits comfortably in the frame from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on a vertical line, keeping the base level along a horizontal one. Include a little of the water in the bottom of the frame for foreground. For a detail shot, zoom in on the raised hand and shield or on a lion head pouring water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright sky or the bronze to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the figure keeps its detail rather than turning into a dark shape. A Live Photo can catch the moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the bronze and granite better than harsh midday sun. Go when the water is flowing for the best foreground.

text.access_note: The fountain stands in Grand Circus Park; check local information before you go for any works or closures.
claims_not_in_sources: The fountain may be switched off or drained at some times of year, so the water may not always be flowing.
Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters bronze and stone better than harsh midday sun.
